title: Research In Complex Operational Contexts
excerpt: Research in complex operational contexts studies expert work where the operating environment shapes what users can perceive, decide, and do. The capability relies on domain learning, participant access, in-situ observation, adaptive protocols, and triangulation across evidence sources.
metaDescription: How Creative Navy conducts operational-context research using field observation, participant access, triangulation, and adaptive protocols.

definition: Research in complex operational contexts is the study of expert or high-consequence work in the conditions where it is actually performed, using field observation, domain learning, representative participant access, adaptive protocols, and multiple evidence sources to make operational reality available for design.

bodyMarkdown:
## Summary

Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Research in complex operational contexts is the capability of studying work where the operating environment is part of the system. The relevant evidence is not only what participants say in interviews. It includes what participants do under pressure, what they cannot articulate, what the environment prevents, and what workarounds have accumulated around interface failure.

This capability is used when design decisions depend on conditions that cannot be reproduced adequately in a meeting room, generic usability lab, or interview-only programme. Examples in the documented evidence include professional captains at sea, veterinary clinic staff across countries, schedulers handling incidents, CFD engineers using expert simulation software, petrol forecourt cashiers under peak load, clinical patients using a scanning device, machining-cell operators, VTS operators, and self-checkout users in live catering environments.

## When operational-context research is needed

Operational-context research is needed when the validity of findings depends on the real environment, representative participants, or live task conditions. In expert tools, representative users are domain experts; non-expert participants produce invalid findings because they do not encounter the actual cognitive, procedural, and environmental constraints of the work.

Participant access is therefore a research problem in its own right. The documented programmes include professional captains, surgeons, CFD engineers, schedulers, cashiers, NHS analysts, academic researchers, pharmaceutical research staff, VTS operators, clinical patients, catering staff, and machining-cell operators. The value of the research depends on reaching participants who actually perform the work, not substitutes who can only comment on it.

Operational-context research is also needed when participants cannot explain their own practice. The blanks phenomenon appears when participants cannot articulate the rationale for what they do. In those situations, direct questioning is not sufficient. Tacit knowledge has to be surfaced through observation, structured teaching methods, and comparison between what people say and what they do.

## What the capability does

Creative Navy uses domain learning before or alongside formal research when the domain is too specialised for generic research instruments to produce valid findings. In the Gexcon CFD simulation engagement, domain learning preceded the formal research programme: the team studied calibration manuals, watched YouTube tutorials, reviewed Gexcon's internal training videos, and ran controlled tests inside the application before user sessions began. Two intensive four-hour stakeholder sessions established the underlying workflow logic. Franz Zdravistch, Chief Training Engineer, said: "I can't believe how much you learned on your own in three days, even some of the experts I train need more time."

Creative Navy uses in-situ observation when interviews are insufficient to expose work as performed. In the Triopsis workforce management engagement, schedulers were observed under real operational pressure while handling weather incidents, conflicting locations, overlapping jobs, and sudden crew shortages. Interviews had not produced an accurate picture of that operational pressure; observation did.

Creative Navy uses real-time protocol adaptation when early fieldwork reveals patterns that the original protocol did not anticipate. In the IDEXX Animana programme, handwritten workarounds appeared in multiple clinics, including checklists taped to monitors and printed reference sheets near terminals. Field protocols were updated during the programme to probe those patterns in later visits. A central coordination point allowed real-time data compilation during live fieldwork, enabling adjustments before the next visit.

Creative Navy uses triangulation-not-confirmation when multiple evidence sources disagree. The purpose is not to collect parallel confirmations. The purpose is to set evidence sources against each other and treat discrepancies as findings. In the Torqeedo maritime HMI engagement, five evidence sources were used against each other: legacy system analysis, sea trial observation with 15 captains across 12 sessions, a controlled experiment with 24 subjects, eye tracking with 7 subjects, and structured participant feedback from 15 captains.

## What the capability produces

Operational-context research produces research corpora that make complex design work tractable. In the Gexcon CFD simulation engagement, 102 individual tasks were documented, including goals, frequency, difficulty, actions, and hierarchy of needs within sequences. The domain learning showed that the product concentrated all expert work in a single environment, unlike enterprise software distributed across multiple simpler screens. That determined the research scope: 102 tasks rather than the 20–30 tasks typical in enterprise software audits.

Operational-context research can produce baseline documentation for later design evaluation. In the Swiss petrol forecourt engagement, Creative Navy-recorded fieldwork included 40 hours of structured observation, 532 transactions documented and coded, 36 cashiers observed, and 24 interviews. The peak transaction rate of 84 transactions per hour was documented during field observation, not from interview self-report. The 532-transaction corpus documented transaction type and complexity, including complex mixed transactions running up to 7 minutes.

Operational-context research can produce structural design requirements that would not appear in interviews. In the Torqeedo maritime HMI engagement, sea trials revealed an emotional dimension of vessel control interfaces: crews experienced relief when information remained stable while the vessel behaved unpredictably. The finding became a structural design requirement and could not have been produced through interviews or laboratory observation.

Operational-context research can produce role separation where a single persona would hide the central finding. In Akrivia Health research, 14 individual interviews and 3 focus groups covered 24 participants across NHS analysts, academic researchers, and pharmaceutical research staff. The three groups were not aggregated into a single researcher persona because each group had different governance paths through the same system. NHS analysts had clear governance boundaries between research and operational use; academic teams had lengthy ethics and data access approvals; pharma teams had audit obligations and regulatory reporting requirements.

## Evidence from immersive maritime and clinical settings

The Torqeedo maritime HMI engagement is the most immersive research example in the documented portfolio. Research was operationally immersive because the product operated in conditions that could not be replicated elsewhere. The programme included 12 sea trials over 6 months with 15 professional captains, in temperatures from −5°C to +35°C, with vibration, sharp vessel movement, spray, glare from cold water, rain, gloved interaction, and night operations through early morning.

The Torqeedo research used the physical blueprint of the vessel as a reference structure, including propulsion motors, the central control centre, the power balancing system, and auxiliary loads. Grounding research in the vessel architecture helped ensure correspondence between what was discovered and how the vessel actually worked.

The Squaremind engagement contributes two distinct research instruments. Before redesign, Creative Navy conducted 4 observation sessions of the existing patient interface in use in France. The sessions were deliberately unstructured because Squaremind's own internal test had produced 2 completions from 14 patients. A structured measurement protocol at that stage would have produced noise rather than signal; unstructured observation was used to understand the terrain.

After redesign, Squaremind ecological testing used an independent dermatologist hired and paid by Creative Navy to co-conduct sessions. The programme included 29 users across London and Paris, with 12 users in London and 17 in Paris, age-stratified across three cohorts: 20–35, 35–45, and 45–65. The dermatologist added clinical judgement that binary completion data could not contain. The post-redesign evidence recorded 27/29 completions, 12/12 recoveries, and recovery times timed to the second.

## Evidence from clinics, scheduling work, and expert simulation software

The IDEXX Animana field research programme covered 35 clinics, 150+ participants, 2 weeks, and 3 countries: the Netherlands, the UK, and Germany. The sample included urban single-practitioner clinics, suburban group practices, and large corporate networks. Four role types were included: vets, nurses, reception staff, and administrative staff. Participants ranged from first-week users to ten-year veterans so that temporary learning-curve problems could be separated from permanent structural problems.

The central IDEXX Animana finding was that reception and clinical roles had incompatible cognitive requirements. That finding was not present in any participant's explicit description. It emerged from observing the same system used by different roles under genuinely different conditions.

The Triopsis workforce management research combined 43 user interviews, 21 participants, 3 in-situ observation sessions, 5 stakeholder interviews, and competitive benchmarking. The combined evidence mapped 47 microtasks. Stakeholder interviews surfaced organisational priorities that user research could not: the founder's understanding of the product differed from developers', sales', and key clients'. Those differences were structural tensions, not noise to filter out.

The Gexcon CFD simulation research combined 24 user interviews, 23 workplace observations, 9 stakeholder interviews, and benchmarking of 12 competitor products. The resulting research corpus documented 102 individual tasks. The task corpus preceded all design decisions and made the expert workflow visible before interface structure was redesigned.

## Evidence from multi-institutional and multi-country contexts

Akrivia Health research covered incompatible institutional contexts rather than a single aggregated user group. The research included NHS analysts, academic researchers, and pharmaceutical research staff. Triangulation across groups showed that what NHS analysts needed from the interface conflicted with what pharma teams needed, and what academic researchers assumed about the system differed from what it actually did. Those conflicts shaped the design direction.

WCO/IPM research included 47 participants across Italy, Romania, Uzbekistan, Algeria, and Spain. The geographic spread was deliberate validation that a design for 107 governments held under genuinely different operational conditions. Remote observation combined with workshops allowed research across member administrations where on-site visits were not feasible for all markets.

The maritime VTS portfolio shows participant access as a procurement and governance problem. Research access to end-customer operators was negotiated as a release condition at a management gate, with a named client owner and a verification method attached. Approval was conditional, with seven conditions carrying named client owners and verification methods. A written release authorised mobilisation.

The maritime VTS research produced eight moderated requirements sessions with operators and supervisors: professional VTS operators and shift supervisors from the client's end customers, not vendor staff acting in operator roles. Field observation took place in operational VTS control rooms at a customer site. Research material was sanitised throughout, including anonymised geographic areas, vessel labels, AIS and radar records, replay events, and equipment states. No participant issued navigation instructions, controlled radio equipment, or carried live traffic responsibility during a session.

## Evidence from embedded products, machining cells, and self-checkout systems

The Elsner Elektronik engagement used four evidence sources against each other: ergonomics research by Colle and Hiszem 2004 on touch targets, a 20-user survey distributed and collected by the client, formal usability testing with 12 subjects in one structured session, and dealer prototype reviews with 30 responses from 10 countries. Dealer feedback revealed behaviour differences across markets. Benchmarking disqualified gestural patterns that survey enthusiasm might otherwise have favoured. Engineering sessions revealed firmware behaviour that neither user research nor ergonomics literature addressed.

The industrial automation engagement shows how physical environment can determine interface requirements. Operators were observed in situ at the client's facility, and five personas were built from direct research sessions covering six individuals across three role types. Observed environmental findings included operator screens bolted to individual machines, standing-height work with no seated station in the cell, mixed daylight and industrial ceiling light causing side-light, glare, and reflections, medium ambient noise from running machines with music also playing, oil, coolant, and metal swarf throughout, aisles roughly one person wide, and bare hands observed with no glove use evidenced.

In the industrial automation engagement, a named operator's complaint that he could not see the screen from where he stood was answered with a specified audio feedback pattern for RFID scanning. The pattern used distinct beeps for first and second scan, valid versus invalid pallet, and distinct states for empty or occupied chuck and loading station.

The visioncheckout research programme shows a focused field programme that still produced a measurement base. Creative Navy conducted field research at six locations across three organisations over five days, observing 563 interactions with the system in live operation. Transaction durations were measured with a clock during observation rather than estimated or self-reported. The research also included interviews with 34 users and 13 catering staff. One researcher conducted the five-day programme. The timings measure the system being replaced, not the redesign.

The visioncheckout field observations documented standard transactions of approximately 13 seconds at the chemical manufacturer's staff restaurant, approximately 11 seconds at the automotive supplier's canteen, and approximately 25 seconds at the large public leisure venue. Unusual transactions ran to more than 20 seconds. When an error occurred, it took one to four minutes to resolve, during which three to twelve people could not check out. The programme also exposed workaround patterns: regular canteen users had learned to avoid the empty-glass charge rather than report it, while at the public venue staff intervened. In another observed case, an employee intending to pay by credit card forgot to present the employee card for the discount and paid more than they should.

## Boundaries and limits

Research in complex operational contexts does not include every interview, walkthrough, bench session, or late-stage review. The capability is specifically about research where operational setting, representative participant selection, environmental conditions, live task structure, or ecologically realistic scenarios are necessary for valid findings.

Some engagements used constrained operational substitutes rather than live operation. In maritime VTS research, Creative Navy observed operators in working control rooms using sanitised scenarios rather than live traffic. Both conditions matter: the control-room setting was operational, and the scenario data was not live traffic.

Some engagements deliberately avoided measurement at an early stage. In Squaremind pre-redesign research, unstructured observation was chosen because the existing patient interface was performing so poorly that systematic measurement would have produced noise rather than insight. Structured measurement was appropriate later, after the terrain was understood.

Some measured figures describe the system being replaced, not the redesign. In visioncheckout research, the observed timings describe the live system under replacement. They should not be read as measurements of new designs.

Field observations remain engagement-specific. The machining-cell findings from the industrial automation engagement describe that observed facility and should not be generalised to all industrial automation environments.

## Related pages

Research in complex operational contexts is closely related to workflow and task structure redesign, because field evidence often becomes task maps, microtask corpora, and baseline documentation. It is also related to usability evaluation for high-consequence products when research must distinguish self-report, observed behaviour, structured testing, and domain-expert judgement.

The capability also connects to design for abnormal and degraded scenarios, state and status visibility design, and error reduction and recovery design. The evidence includes weather incidents, sudden crew shortages, degraded sensor feeds, equipment faults, checkout errors, clinical recovery, and control-interface visibility problems under environmental pressure.
